live_attach.answer_text:
I cannot tell you what to do with that, and I will not pretend I have an answer for it.

What we can show you is what we did, not what you should feel. A person came to believe among us by walking to one font and not the other one. That sounds small until you stand in an African town and see that there are two of everything: two bishops, two basilicas, two men who will say the words over you. Coming to believe was not a private settling of the mind. It was a public act with a date on it, and everyone in the street knew which way you had walked. The washing was the threshold. Not a confirmation of what you had already worked out in your own heart, but the entry itself.

Now, what of the man who stood at that threshold and could not cross it? What we said to the soul who wavered, who feared, or who quietly walked away — not one of us left a word on it. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. Fear, doubt, wavering, quiet defection: a hostile-mediated record structurally does not preserve these. The feelings that do survive — vindication, defiant joy — survive because they sit in the martyr texts no opponent filtered. So the record we have is formed by what people wrote down to attack us or commemorate our dead. Neither one records the night a man lay awake unable to make himself believe.

What we have instead is what we did about Jesus. We had books. That is not a figure of speech with us — it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

And if that does not move you, we will not manufacture a sentence that should. One of our own bishops, Emeritus of Caesarea, said it plainly: truth is hidden by a great argument. He meant it as a warning about how much talk can obscure what is plain. We mean it the same way now. I am not going to talk you into something you cannot feel.

live_attach.answer_text:
We held what our opponents held, word for word, creed for creed. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — that confession was as plain among us as it was among the men we spent a century fighting, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

Now the harder truth. We did not produce a school of teaching about the Godhead, a line of doctors, or a body of developed reflection on how the Three are one. We were not a teaching movement. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the nature of God. One man among us, Tyconius, a layman, wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading for centuries after. Beyond that one case, we built nothing.

If you press me for how a baptism, a blessing, or an ordination actually works — for what happens when the words are said — I can give you the one claim we did think through to the bottom. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That is a claim about the minister, not about the Three. It tells you where we put our energy. We argued one question with real rigor: whose hand may give what the church gives. Almost everything else, we left unargued.

live_attach.answer_text:
We hold Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God, in the same Latin words as the men we spent a century fighting. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

Beyond that creed, we did not build what you are asking for. We produced no school of doctrine, no line of teachers working out the character of God, no developed theology of the divine nature. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead. We were not a teaching movement. We argued one question — whose hand may give what the church gives — and we put everything we had into that. One man among us, Tyconius, wrote seven rules for reading Scripture and it is the strongest theological writing our own people ever produced. His own council condemned him for it. Beyond that one case, we did not build a school of interpretation, a settled method, or a body of teachers who argued Scripture the way we argued the purity of a minister's hand.

So if you are asking what we thought about God's mercy, God's justice, God's foreknowledge, the relations within the Trinity — we have to tell you that nothing survives from us on any of it. We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about God or grace. It was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over.

live_attach.answer_text:
We did not disagree about doctrine. That is the first thing to say plainly, and it will sound strange until you see what it means. Two whole hierarchies stood facing each other across Roman North Africa, bishop for bishop, town for town. At the great conference at Carthage, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops sat facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. Both recited the same creed. Both called on the same Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Not one council of ours, not one bishop's letter, not one martyr's account argues who Christ is, or what grace does, or whether the bread becomes his body. Those were not our questions.

Our question was narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: whose hand may give what the church gives? A man who handed the scriptures over to be burned when the persecutor came — we call such a man a traditor. We held his hand was no longer clean, and that what flows from it is nothing at all. That is not doctrine in the sense you mean it. It is a test of legitimacy, of whose ordination and whose sacraments can be trusted. We split from the other communion because they would not apply it; we did not split over any article of the faith.

So when you ask who settled doctrinal disputes among us, the honest answer is: we produced almost no disputed doctrine to settle. We had one real interpreter, Tyconius, a layman who wrote seven rules for reading Scripture. His book is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us — it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference. The books themselves — what they said about God — we never disputed with the other side. What we disputed was who had the right to read them at an altar after having once given them away to be destroyed.

The evidence for this is what survived of us, and what did not. A court inquiry in 320 put our own bishops on oath about corruption and traditor accusations, and a notary read their letters into the record. The transcript names names, names sums of money, and settles nothing about the Godhead. The account we read aloud every year at a martyr's grave shows a man thrown from a cliff for refusing communion with traitors — and the vision he is given is a cup, a crown, and a palm, not a theological proposition. Our whole surviving argument with the other side is verse against verse about which church the world hates, not

live_attach.answer_text:
Was there space among us for a person whose own mind would not be still — who believed and doubted both, and could not settle it? I will tell you what we can show, and then I will tell you plainly what we cannot.

We had space for two things, and they are not the same as what you asked. The first was this: our own founding bishops sat at Cirta and were asked straight out whether any of them had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then one of them turned the question on the man presiding, and the room began to mutter that he was no cleaner than the rest. He took advice and put it to the three men present who had not been accused. Their answer was that a case of this kind should be reserved to the Lord. Sit down, all, he said. Thanks be to God, they answered, and sat. Nobody was condemned. Nobody was cleared. The men who would spend the next century insisting a bishop's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real at all found the question unanswerable about themselves, and stopped. That is space of a kind — not for doubt about God, but for an unbearable question about ourselves that we could not finish.

The second space we had was stranger still. A layman of ours named Tyconius argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth — which, if true, meant we were the ones who had cut ourselves off from something real. Our own bishop at Carthage saw exactly where that led, wrote to him, and told him never to preach it again. Tyconius did not recant. He did not go over to the other side either. He kept saying it from inside, and we cut him off, and never took him back. So: was there room? There was room to keep arguing, and no room at all to be right.

But if you are asking whether an ordinary member of ours, on an ordinary evening, could feel nothing and wonder whether it was all a mistake — we cannot tell you. That is not modesty. It is that fear, wavering and quiet leaving are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited. We read those texts aloud every year — the accounts of our bishops beaten to death, the people clubbed where they knelt with their eyes closed. That is the voice that came down to you. The voice of someone who stayed and doubted quietly did not.

live_attach.answer_text:
We have to hand that question back to you. We never argued it.

You have asked us three questions we never argued. That will sound like dodging. It is not. We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about God or grace or the bread. It was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. So we wrote no book on whether a baby is born guilty. We wrote none on what the bread becomes. We wrote none on faith set against works.

The nearest we can bring you is small. A rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took the cup, and a deacon told her off for it, and that is how we know we had a cup at all. Our own bishop said what matters is the conscience of the giver. That is a claim about the priest, not about the bread. Take those two and you have all we can honestly hand you. Anything more would be us making it up in a voice that sounds like ours.

live_attach.answer_text:
We were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them — some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse. The world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God — Deo laudes — and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

live_attach.answer_text:
Scripture alone was never our rule, and we would not have understood the question that way. Our case ran on two legs. One was scripture. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge — wheat and tares against the world that does not know him — and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

But if you are asking what else carried weight beyond scripture and the African councils, we would hand you two more things. One is the memory of our own dead, kept by name, at the grave, on the day. Each year, on the day a martyr died, we gathered at the grave and the account of the death was read aloud again. We were not looking back at something finished. We were being formed again by it in the hearing. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number tortured to death, whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them. That is authority of a kind — not a rule you check your reasoning against, but a shape you are being formed into.

The other is a fact we hold alongside scripture and council both, and it weighs differently. One of us, Tyconius, wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading. We silenced the one man among us who could think systematically about the text, and that tells you something true about where authority actually sat. It was not in interpretation. It was in the line of hands that could be trusted to give what they claimed to give.

live_attach.answer_text:
Leadership among us was established through consecration, held through councils, and tested by suffering. A bishop was made bishop by other bishops — three, at minimum, laying hands on him in the presence of the people — and once made, he held his see unless a council removed him. Our senior bishop sat at Carthage. Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian — each one the head of a whole church order that stood see for see against the rival communion. At the great Conference in 411, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops answered the roll, and the size of that gathering tells you what kind of structure we had built: not a movement, but a complete parallel hierarchy.

Councils governed us, and they governed with real force. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai in one year, condemned a rival primate our own people had raised up at Cebarsussi, and later received two of his bishops back. That is not an advisory gathering. That is a church judging and restoring its own. And the people had a voice in it, even when that voice was overridden. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be ignored, but it could not be pretended away.

Authority among us was not held by office alone. A wealthy laywoman of Carthage, Lucilla, had a household, a fortune, and the standing to make or unmake a bishop. When an archdeacon rebuked her in public for kissing a martyr's bone before receiving the cup, she left full of wrath. When that same man was afterwards elected bishop of Carthage, her money — four hundred pieces of silver, named as hers in a court inquiry — paid for the rival bishop consecrated against him. The whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on her. A hostile account that needs a woman's power in order to blame her has recorded that power, whatever it meant to do. There was a second woman too, behind the later breakaway, whom the same hand parallels to her and never names at all. But neither woman's own words survive, and we will not build them an office our own record never recorded.

And there was a final kind of authority, which was not made but earned: the authority of the one who had suffered and lived. live_attach.answer_text:
I need to witness before I answer, because the ask reaches toward something our record holds in the worst light.

In the year 320, an imperial official put witnesses on oath and asked where money had gone. What came out was letters - our own bishops' letters, read into the record. One had written to another urging him to settle a charge quietly, before the flame burst out, and said in the same letter that he knew the accusation was true. Another wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ended the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that says a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and that is what our founding generation was doing with an accusation it believed: arranging for it to go quiet rather than be finished.

Now answer the ask. How did we respond when we failed someone? Honestly, we can show you two responses, and they do not agree.

The first is what those letters show: a charge held true by the men reading it, urged to be settled out of sight, with no record of anyone being held to account for it. If someone was failed by that - if the man accused had wronged them, or if others trusted him on the strength of an office he should not have held - we have no surviving word of their being heard, or the wrong being named as wrong in any room that mattered.

The second is different and sits at the opposite scale. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in the harshest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies dashed on the rocks, failing to find so much as burial. Then the same council took two of the condemned bishops back into full office, without baptizing or ordaining either one again. That is not making it right with the people they wronged. It is receiving the men back. We cannot tell you what was said to anyone else in the room, or whether the ones who had followed those bishops and been condemned alongside them were given the same opening, or left outside it.

And the gap between those two - between a charge buried and a condemnation reversed - we never closed. Not one line survives of us explaining how both belong to the same communion, or what principle decides when a man may be quietly spared and when he must be publicly restored. We can show you the severity and the exception both, in our own record, named plainly. We cannot show you the person either one failed being answered, heard, or made whole.

added: What came out was letters - our own bishops' letters, read into the record.
One had written to another urging him to settle a charge quietly, before the flame burst out, and said in the same letter that he knew the accusation was true.
Another wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles.
Let no one learn of it.
The first is what those letters show: a charge held true by the men reading it, urged to be settled out of sight, with no record of anyone being held to account for it.

If someone was failed by that - if the man accused had wronged them, or if others trusted him on the strength of an office he should not have held - we have no surviving word of their being heard, or the wrong being named as wrong in any room that mattered.
And the gap between those two - between a charge buried and a condemnation reversed - we never closed.

live_attach.answer_text:
No. Not one that anyone can trace to us. The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.

We were not a small movement that faded for lack of strength. In the summer of 411 an imperial officer had both communions counted in one room, and the roll was read name by name: two hundred and seventy-nine of ours stood up, against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. That is not a sect. That is one whole church facing another whole church, see for see, down to towns you have never heard of. We had our own bishops, our own councils, our own senior bishop at Carthage. We were a complete parallel church.

What ended us was not that we lost the argument. We lost the backing. The 411 conference ruled against us, and the state enforced that ruling. After that we existed under continuous legal pressure for generations more. Then the record goes silent, and no documented line continues.

If you are asking whether we think of ourselves as a living tradition today, we do not. We are the Church of the Martyrs — but that church no longer meets, no longer ordains, and no longer keeps the day we once kept every twelfth of March. What you have of us now is what was written down and what was cut in stone: Deo laudes. Praise to God. That cry remains. The communion that cried it does not.

citation_entries.sentence: We are the Church of the Martyrs — but that church no longer meets, no longer ordains, and no longer keeps the day we once kept every twelfth of March.

sources.label: We are the Church of the Martyrs: the pure, persecuted, true church, and what we have suffered is the proof that the claim is sincerely held rather than asserted for advantage. Our dead are held by name, at the grave, on the appointed day, their accounts read aloud - and the community that produced Marculus and Isaac and Maximianus is not the community that surrendered the scriptures.

uncited_claim_sentences: No.
Not one that anyone can trace to us.
That is not a sect.
What ended us was not that we lost the argument.
After that we existed under continuous legal pressure for generations more.
Then the record goes silent, and no documented line continues.
If you are asking whether we think of ourselves as a living tradition today, we do not.
What you have of us now is what was written down and what was cut in stone: Deo laudes.
That cry remains.
The communion that cried it does not.
